title: SQL Query Detective
description: Work out what each query returns and find the bug when it returns the wrong result. The quiz covers joins, fan-out, NULL, aggregation, and misleading filters. Unless stated otherwise, assume standard SQL behavior. Without `ORDER BY`, row order does not matter.

questions.title: How many rows does this inner join return?
questions.description:
Tables:

- `customers`: `(1, 'Ada')`, `(2, 'Lin')`, `(3, 'Sam')`
- `orders`: `(101, 1)`, `(102, 1)`, `(103, 3)`, `(104, NULL)`

Columns are `customers(id, name)` and `orders(id, customer_id)`.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
```

Enter the number of result rows.
questions.explanation: Ada matches orders 101 and 102. Sam matches order 103. Lin has no order, and order 104 has a NULL `customer_id`, so neither produces a row. The query returns 3 rows.

questions.title: Which customer names survive this query?
questions.description:
Using the same `customers` and `orders` data, suppose orders also contain `status`: order 101 is `paid`, 102 is `pending`, 103 is `pending`, and 104 is `paid`.

```sql
SELECT c.name
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
```

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join invents NULL rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: The left panel: the invented NULL row fails the `WHERE` test.

questions.explanation: The `LEFT JOIN` first keeps Lin and fills the order columns with NULL. The `WHERE` clause then removes that row because `NULL = 'paid'` is unknown, not true. Ada remains because order 101 is paid. Sam's only order is pending. For this filter, the query behaves like an inner join.

questions.title: What rows does moving the paid filter into `ON` produce?
questions.description:
The data is the same as in the previous Question.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND o.status = 'paid';
```

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join invents NULL rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: The right panel: in `ON`, the filter decides matching, not survival.

questions.explanation: The `ON` clause limits which orders can match, but the left join still keeps every customer. Ada matches paid order 101. Lin and Sam have no paid order, so their order columns are NULL. Order 104 has no customer id and matches nobody.

questions.title: What are the counts for customers with no orders?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS rows_seen, COUNT(o.id) AS orders_seen
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
```

Focus on Lin, who has no matching order.
questions.explanation: The left join keeps one row for Lin and fills its order columns with NULL. `COUNT(*)` counts the row, so `rows_seen` is 1. `COUNT(o.id)` ignores the NULL order id, so `orders_seen` is 0.

questions.title: What total does the query report after accidental fan-out?
questions.description:
Order 10 has two items priced 30 and 20, plus three payments of 10 each.

```sql
SELECT SUM(i.price) AS item_total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN payments AS p ON p.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.id = 10;
```

Enter the reported `item_total`.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing — 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times then 20/10 three times — so SUM(i.price) reports 150, each price counted once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, each payment counted once per item; a window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child, and not DISTINCT, which would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: Six rows, and each price counted once per payment.

questions.explanation: Each of the 2 items matches each of the 3 payments, so the joins create `2 × 3 = 6` rows. Each item price appears three times. The query calculates `(30 + 20) × 3 = 150`, although the real item total is 50.

questions.title: Which approaches safely compute both item and payment totals per order?
questions.description: Select every safe approach. Both child tables may contain equal amounts in different rows.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing — 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times then 20/10 three times — so SUM(i.price) reports 150, each price counted once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, each payment counted once per item; a window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child, and not DISTINCT, which would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: Collapse each child to one row per order first.

options.text: Aggregate `order_items` and `payments` separately by `order_id`, then join those one-row-per-order results
Use correlated scalar subqueries that aggregate each child table independently for the current order
Add `DISTINCT` to the final `SELECT` while leaving both raw child joins intact

questions.explanation: Aggregate each child table on its own before joining, or calculate each total in a separate correlated subquery. Both approaches keep the child tables from multiplying each other. `SUM(DISTINCT amount)` is wrong when two real rows have the same amount. A final `DISTINCT` runs too late: `SUM` has already counted the duplicated input rows.

questions.title: What does `NULL = NULL` evaluate to in a SQL predicate?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: UNKNOWN, and a `WHERE` clause keeps only TRUE.

questions.explanation: The result is unknown. NULL means the value is unknown, so SQL cannot prove that two NULL values are equal. A `WHERE` clause keeps only rows where its condition is true.

questions.title: Which standard SQL predicate considers two NULL values equal?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: The green card names the standard predicate.

questions.explanation: `a IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b` is true when `a` and `b` are equal or when both are NULL. It always returns true or false, never unknown. Ordinary equality does not work this way when either value is NULL. Some databases also have their own NULL-safe operators.

questions.title: Which values does this `NOT IN` query return?
questions.description:
Table `candidate(id)` contains `1`, `2`, and `3`. Table `blocked(id)` contains `2` and `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT id
FROM candidate
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM blocked);
```

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: The expansion is what does it: one UNKNOWN poisons the `AND`.

questions.explanation: For ids 1 and 3, the comparison with 2 is unequal, but the comparison with NULL is unknown. That makes `NOT IN` unknown rather than true. For id 2, `NOT IN` is false because 2 is present. `WHERE` keeps only true results, so the query returns no rows.

questions.title: Which values does the `NOT EXISTS` anti-join return?
questions.description:
Use the same `candidate` values `1`, `2`, `3` and `blocked` values `2`, `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT c.id
FROM candidate AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM blocked AS b
  WHERE b.id = c.id
);
```

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: Existence is a yes-or-no question, with no third answer.

questions.explanation: The subquery finds a matching blocked row only for id 2. The NULL in `blocked.id` does not equal any candidate id. It does not affect the other candidates, so ids 1 and 3 pass `NOT EXISTS`.

questions.title: How many rows satisfy `rating <> 5`?
questions.description:
The `rating` values are `5`, `4`, and `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT * FROM reviews WHERE rating <> 5;
```

Enter the row count.

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: `<>` against NULL is UNKNOWN, so those rows never qualify.

questions.explanation: Only rating 4 makes `rating <> 5` true. Rating 5 makes it false, and NULL makes it unknown. To include missing ratings, write that rule explicitly: `rating <> 5 OR rating IS NULL`.

questions.title: Which rows satisfy `COALESCE(discount, 0) = 0`?
questions.description: The `discount` values are `0`, `10`, and `NULL`.
questions.explanation: `COALESCE` returns the first non-NULL argument. A stored 0 stays 0, while NULL becomes 0. Both rows pass the filter. Be careful: this expression treats 'no discount recorded' and 'a recorded discount of zero' as the same thing.

questions.title: What does `SUM(amount)` return when no rows qualify?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT SUM(amount)
FROM payments
WHERE status = 'missing-status';
```

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: `SUM` of nothing is NULL, not zero.

questions.explanation: The query still returns one row because it has no `GROUP BY`. `COUNT` returns 0 for an empty input, but `SUM` and most other aggregates return NULL. Use `COALESCE(SUM(amount), 0)` when zero is the right business value.

questions.title: What does `COUNT(amount)` return when no rows qualify?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: `COUNT` of nothing is zero — the one aggregate that never returns NULL.

questions.explanation: An aggregate query without `GROUP BY` still returns one row when its input is empty. `COUNT(amount)` counts non-NULL amounts. There are none, so it returns 0.

questions.title: What is `AVG(score)` for scores `10`, `20`, and `NULL`?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: The NULL is skipped, in the numerator and the denominator alike.

questions.explanation: `AVG(score)` ignores NULL, so it calculates `(10 + 20) / 2 = 15`. If you replace the missing score with zero, the result becomes 10. That is a different rule and must be written explicitly, for example as `AVG(COALESCE(score, 0))`.

questions.title: What is `COUNT(DISTINCT category)` for `A`, `A`, `B`, and `NULL`?

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: NULL is not a distinct value here.

questions.explanation: The distinct non-NULL values are A and B. `COUNT(expression)` ignores NULL even when used with `DISTINCT`, so the result is 2.

questions.title: How many groups does `GROUP BY region` form?
questions.description: The `region` values are `'east'`, `'east'`, `NULL`, and `NULL`.

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: Grouping is the exception: every NULL lands in one group.

questions.explanation: `GROUP BY` puts the two NULL values in one group. The query therefore creates an `east` group and a NULL group. This differs from ordinary equality, where `NULL = NULL` is unknown.

questions.title: Which customers does this query find?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id
HAVING COUNT(o.id) = 0;
```

options.text: Customers with exactly one matching order
No customers, because a left join always makes `COUNT(*)` positive
Customers whose order ids are duplicated

questions.explanation: A customer without orders still gets one row from the left join, but `o.id` is NULL. `COUNT(o.id)` ignores that NULL and returns 0, so `HAVING` keeps the customer. `COUNT(*)` would return 1 and would not work for this test.

questions.title: Why does this query omit departments with no sales since 2026 began?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT d.id, SUM(s.amount)
FROM departments AS d
LEFT JOIN sales AS s ON s.department_id = d.id
WHERE s.sold_at >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY d.id;
```

options.text: The `WHERE` predicate rejects NULL-extended rows before grouping
`SUM` automatically removes departments whose total is zero
`GROUP BY` cannot group rows produced by a left join
Date predicates are evaluated after aggregation

questions.explanation: The join runs before `WHERE`. A department with no sale since January 1 gets a row where `s.sold_at` is NULL. The date test is then unknown, so `WHERE` removes the row. Put the date condition in `ON` to keep every department.

questions.title: Which clause should filter groups whose total sales exceed 1,000?
questions.explanation: `WHERE` filters rows before SQL forms the groups. `HAVING` filters the completed groups, so `HAVING SUM(amount) > 1000` is the correct condition.

questions.title: What defect causes the duplicated matches?
questions.description:
Prices are unique only by `(sku, region)`. Product `X` has one price row for `US` and one for `EU`. An order line for `(X, US)` is queried with:

```sql
SELECT l.sku, p.amount
FROM order_lines AS l
JOIN prices AS p ON p.sku = l.sku;
```

options.text: The join omits `p.region = l.region` from the composite key
The price table needs a NULL row

questions.explanation: The US order line matches both price rows because the join checks only `sku`. The full key is `(sku, region)`, so the join must also include `p.region = l.region`. Sorting the result would not fix the extra match.

questions.title: Which predicate produces each unordered employee pair exactly once?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT a.id, b.id
FROM employees AS a
JOIN employees AS b ON /* predicate */;
```

Assume employee ids are unique and non-NULL. No employee should pair with themself.
questions.explanation: `a.id < b.id` removes self-pairs and keeps one ordering of each pair. With `a.id <> b.id`, both `(a, b)` and `(b, a)` appear. With `a.id <= b.id`, every employee also pairs with themself.

questions.title: How many rows result from joining students through enrollments?
questions.description:
Student 1 has 2 enrollment rows, student 2 has 3, and student 3 has none. Every enrollment references one existing course.

```sql
SELECT s.id, c.id
FROM students AS s
JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.student_id = s.id
JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id;
```

Enter the result row count.
questions.explanation: Each enrollment links one student to one course, so each enrollment becomes one result row. Students 1 and 2 contribute `2 + 3 = 5` rows. Student 3 has no enrollment and disappears in the inner join. Five rows is correct here because the query asks for student-course pairs.

questions.title: What should you check when a many-to-one join doubles some sales?
questions.description: A sales fact table joins to `stores` on `store_code`. Each sale should match one store, but some sales appear twice.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing — 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times then 20/10 three times — so SUM(i.price) reports 150, each price counted once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, each payment counted once per item; a window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child, and not DISTINCT, which would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: A many-to-one join is only many-to-one if the right side really is unique.

options.text: Whether the join predicate omits part of the store's real key
Whether temporal dimension versions require an effective-date predicate
Whether adding final `DISTINCT` makes the model correct

questions.explanation: The join is not many-to-one in practice if a sale matches two store rows. Check for duplicate `store_code` values, a missing part of the real key, or historical rows that need an effective-date condition. `DISTINCT` can hide some repeated output rows, but it does not fix the relationship or a wrong total.

questions.title: Why is `SELECT DISTINCT` a risky repair for an unexpectedly duplicating join?

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing — 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times then 20/10 three times — so SUM(i.price) reports 150, each price counted once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, each payment counted once per item; a window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child, and not DISTINCT, which would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: `DISTINCT` cannot tell a duplicate from two items priced the same.

options.text: It can hide a wrong join cardinality instead of fixing the relationship
It removes rows based only on projected columns, which may collapse legitimate records
It cannot undo inflation already used inside an aggregate expression
It guarantees one output row per left-table key

questions.explanation: `DISTINCT` compares the columns in the final result. Two real records can look identical after projection and be collapsed, while bad join matches that differ in one column remain. It also cannot fix `SUM(...)`: the aggregate has already read the duplicated rows before final deduplication.

questions.title: Which rows can match because of missing parentheses?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT *
FROM users AS u
JOIN events AS e
  ON e.user_id = u.id
 AND e.kind = 'purchase'
  OR e.kind = 'signup';
```

options.text: Every signup event can match every user, regardless of `user_id`
Signup events match only when `e.user_id = u.id`
No rows, because `AND` and `OR` cannot appear together in `ON`

questions.explanation: `AND` is evaluated before `OR`. SQL reads the condition as `(e.user_id = u.id AND e.kind = 'purchase') OR e.kind = 'signup'`. A signup event therefore matches every user. Parentheses fix it: `e.user_id = u.id AND (e.kind = 'purchase' OR e.kind = 'signup')`.

questions.title: How many rows does the full outer join return?
questions.description:
Table `a(k)` contains `1`, `2`, `2`; table `b(k)` contains `2`, `2`, `3`.

```sql
SELECT a.k, b.k
FROM a
FULL OUTER JOIN b ON b.k = a.k;
```

Enter the row count.
questions.explanation: Each of the two rows where `a.k = 2` matches both rows where `b.k = 2`. That produces `2 × 2 = 4` rows. The unmatched value 1 from `a` adds one row, and the unmatched value 3 from `b` adds another. The total is 6.

questions.title: How many rows do `UNION ALL` and `UNION` return?
questions.description: Query X yields values `1, 1, 2`; query Y yields `2, 3`. Consider `X UNION ALL Y` and `X UNION Y`.
questions.explanation: `UNION ALL` keeps every row: three from X and two from Y, for 5 rows. `UNION` removes duplicate result rows, leaving 1, 2, and 3, for 3 rows.

questions.title: How many rows does a cross join produce?
questions.description:
Table `sizes` has 4 rows and table `colors` has 6 rows.

```sql
SELECT * FROM sizes CROSS JOIN colors;
```
questions.explanation: A cross join pairs every size with every color. The result has `4 × 6 = 24` rows. That is useful when you want every combination and a bug when you do not.

questions.title: Why do authors without books disappear from this join chain?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT a.name, p.name
FROM authors AS a
LEFT JOIN books AS b ON b.author_id = a.id
JOIN publishers AS p ON p.id = b.publisher_id;
```

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join invents NULL rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: The inner join afterwards has nothing to match a NULL key against.

options.text: The inner join to `publishers` rejects the NULL book row
A left join cannot be followed by another join
The database evaluates the publisher join before the author join
Authors without books are grouped away

questions.explanation: The left join keeps an author without books and fills the `b` columns with NULL. The inner join then tests `p.id = b.publisher_id`. No publisher matches the NULL value, so the author disappears. Use another left join for `publishers` if authors without books must remain.

questions.title: Does a NULL join value match another NULL join value?
questions.description: Assume the join uses ordinary equality: `left.value = right.value`.

images.alt: Cards on SQL's three-valued logic. NULL = NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN, so two NULL join keys never match, and rating <> 5 is UNKNOWN when rating is NULL, so that row is dropped too; IS NOT DISTINCT FROM is the standard null-safe comparison, true when both sides are NULL. With candidate holding 1, 2 and 3 and blocked holding 2 and NULL, id NOT IN (2, NULL) expands to id <> 2 AND id <> NULL, whose second half is UNKNOWN for every row, so no rows come back, while NOT EXISTS asks a yes-or-no question and returns 1 and 3. Over no qualifying rows SUM returns NULL and COUNT returns 0; over rows including a NULL, AVG of 10, 20 and NULL is 15 and COUNT(DISTINCT c) of A, A, B and NULL is 2. Grouping is the one place NULLs count as equal: GROUP BY collects every NULL into a single group.
images.caption: Two NULL keys compare as UNKNOWN, so they never join.

options.text: No; ordinary equality with NULL is unknown
Yes; joins automatically match NULL with NULL
Yes, but only in an inner join

questions.explanation: Join conditions use the same NULL rules as other SQL conditions. `NULL = NULL` is unknown, not true, so the two rows do not match under ordinary equality.

questions.title: Why does a window total repeat an inflated value after a join?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT o.id,
       SUM(i.price) OVER (PARTITION BY o.id) AS item_total
FROM orders AS o
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
JOIN shipments AS s ON s.order_id = o.id;
```

One order has 2 items and 3 shipments.

images.alt: Order 10 in three tables: one orders row, two order_items priced 30 and 20 with a true total of 50, and three payments of 10 with a true total of 30. Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing — 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times then 20/10 three times — so SUM(i.price) reports 150, each price counted once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, each payment counted once per item; a window function over those rows inflates the same way. A green card gives the repair: aggregate each child by order_id separately and join the results, or use one correlated scalar subquery per child, and not DISTINCT, which would collapse two items genuinely priced 20 into one. A final note says fan-out begins at the first join whose right side has more than one row per join key.
images.caption: The window sees the six duplicated rows, not the two real ones.

options.text: Window functions operate on the six joined rows, after fan-out has occurred
Window functions always multiply sums by the number of tables
`PARTITION BY` performs a distinct aggregation first
The window frame excludes item rows

questions.explanation: The joins create `2 × 3 = 6` rows before the window function runs. Each item price now appears three times, once per shipment. The window sum reads all six rows and repeats the inflated total on each one. A window function keeps the input rows; it does not undo fan-out.

questions.title: What is guaranteed by `SELECT id FROM tasks LIMIT 1` without `ORDER BY`?

options.text: At most one qualifying row, but not which row

questions.explanation: `LIMIT 1` guarantees no more than one row. It does not choose which row. Without `ORDER BY`, the database may return any qualifying row, and a different query plan may choose another one.

questions.title: Which 2026 rows can an inclusive `BETWEEN` filter accidentally omit?
questions.description:
```sql
WHERE created_at BETWEEN TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00'
                     AND TIMESTAMP '2026-12-31 00:00:00'
```

options.text: Rows later than midnight on December 31, 2026
Rows exactly at midnight on December 31, 2026

questions.explanation: `BETWEEN` includes both endpoints, but the upper endpoint is midnight at the start of December 31. Every later time that day is greater and gets excluded. Use a half-open range instead: `created_at >= TIMESTAMP '2026-01-01 00:00:00' AND created_at < TIMESTAMP '2027-01-01 00:00:00'`.

questions.title: Why does this expression count every row?
questions.description:
```sql
COUNT(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
```

options.text: `COUNT(expression)` counts both 1 and 0 because both are non-NULL
`CASE` cannot be used inside an aggregate
Zero is equivalent to NULL in SQL

questions.explanation: `COUNT(expression)` counts every non-NULL result. This `CASE` returns either 1 or 0, so it never returns NULL and every row is counted. Remove `ELSE 0` so non-paid rows return NULL, or use `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'paid' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

questions.title: What does `SUM(CASE WHEN paid THEN amount END)` return when no row is paid?

options.text: A syntax error because `ELSE` is mandatory

questions.explanation: Without `ELSE`, the `CASE` returns NULL for every non-paid row. If no row is paid, `SUM` receives only NULL values and returns NULL. Add `ELSE 0` or wrap the sum in `COALESCE` when you need zero.

questions.title: When is `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL` a reliable anti-join?

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join invents NULL rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: Reliable only when that column cannot itself be NULL.

options.text: When the tested right-side column is guaranteed non-NULL on every genuine match
Whenever any nullable right-side column is tested
Only when the left table has no primary key
Only when both tables are empty

questions.explanation: An unmatched left row gets NULL in every right-side column. Test a right-side column that can never be NULL on a real match, such as a non-NULL key. If you test a nullable column, a real match with NULL in that column can look like an unmatched row.

questions.title: What happens when a left-table filter is placed inside the `ON` clause?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.id, o.id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id
 AND c.active = TRUE;
```

Some customers are inactive.

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join invents NULL rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). Further cards note that a filter on the left table inside ON removes nothing, only preventing matches; that an inner join after a left join cannot match a NULL key, so authors without books vanish again; that counting only some children while keeping every parent means filtering in ON or pre-filtering the child in a subquery; and that LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.key IS NULL is a reliable anti-join only when that column is genuinely NOT NULL.
images.caption: It stops the match, not the row.

options.text: Inactive customers remain, but with NULL order columns
Inactive customers are removed from the result
The query is invalid because `ON` cannot reference the left table

questions.explanation: In a left join, `ON` decides whether a right row matches. It does not remove rows from the left table. An inactive customer fails the match condition but still appears with NULL order columns. Put `c.active = TRUE` in `WHERE` if inactive customers should disappear.

questions.title: What is wrong with grouping by both customer and order when one row per customer is required?
questions.description:
```sql
SELECT c.id, o.id, SUM(i.amount)
FROM customers AS c
JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
GROUP BY c.id, o.id;
```

options.text: The query's grain is one row per customer-order pair, not one row per customer
`SUM` cannot be used with two grouping columns
Grouping by an order id combines all customers
The joins must be cross joins for aggregation

questions.explanation: The grouping columns define the level of each result row. Because `o.id` is included, the query returns one row per customer and order, not one row per customer. Remove the order id from both `SELECT` and `GROUP BY` to calculate a customer-level total.

questions.title: Does a group containing only NULL scores pass `HAVING AVG(score) >= 0`?

options.text: No; `AVG(score)` is NULL and the comparison is unknown
Yes; an all-NULL average is zero
Yes; NULL is greater than every number
The aggregate query always throws an error

questions.explanation: `AVG` ignores NULL values. With no non-NULL scores, the average itself is NULL. `NULL >= 0` is unknown, and `HAVING` keeps only groups where the condition is true, so this group is removed.

questions.title: Which checks help find where unexpected fan-out begins?

Joining both children to the same parent produces every pairing — 2 × 3 = 6 rows, listed as 30/10 three times then 20/10 three times — so SUM(i.price) reports 150, each price counted once per payment, and SUM(p.amount) reports 60, each payment counted once per item; a window function over those rows inflates the same way. images.caption: Count rows after each join, and find the first one that multiplies.

options.text: Compare row counts and distinct business keys before and after each join
Group the candidate right-side key and inspect keys with `COUNT(*) > 1`
Temporarily select the join keys and duplicated entity ids for a small failing case
Add `ORDER BY` and assume adjacent duplicates prove the rows are identical

questions.explanation: Check the row count and the number of distinct business keys after each join. Then look for duplicate values in the right-side join key. A small failing example shows exactly which rows matched. Sorting may make duplicates easier to see, but it does not prove that two rows mean the same thing.

questions.title: Which rewrite preserves all accounts while counting only successful logins?
questions.description: The result must include accounts with zero successful logins. Assume `logins.id` is non-NULL.

images.alt: Two versions of the same LEFT JOIN over three customers where only Ada has a paid order. With WHERE o.status = 'paid', the join invents NULL rows for Lin and Sam and the WHERE test then discards them, leaving Ada only. With AND o.status = 'paid' inside the ON clause, the filter only decides what counts as a match, so unmatched left rows survive: (Ada, 101), (Lin, NULL), (Sam, NULL). options.text: `LEFT JOIN logins l ON l.account_id = a.id AND l.success = TRUE`, then `COUNT(l.id)`
`LEFT JOIN logins l ON l.account_id = a.id`, then `WHERE l.success = TRUE` and `COUNT(*)`
